title: Lock accounts down, back up, and handle a hacked email

say: Lock accounts down, back up, and handle a hacked email.
This is the video for module 2 of Cybersecurity Fundamentals.
Three cheap tools do most of the protective work: a password manager, multi-factor authentication, which we call MFA, and well set up devices.

say: Each extra word multiplies the attacker's work by 7,776, far more than adding a symbol. Chiamaka chooses six random words.

You memorise only that one. The password manager creates a unique password for every other account, so one leak cannot unlock the rest. Reused passwords are the biggest real cause of account takeover.

say: A password alone is the weakest. SMS codes are better than nothing, but they can be stolen through SIM swap fraud or tricked out of people on the phone.
Authenticator apps make a six-digit code on the phone itself, changing every 30 seconds. Passkeys and security keys go further: they only work on the real website, so a fake login page gets nothing.
Use the strongest method each service offers, at least for email, banking and social media admin. Keep recovery codes on paper, locked away.

The 3-2-1 rule says keep 3 copies of important data. For example, Hauwa runs IT for a 6-person consultancy in Kano. She keeps the working files, a cloud copy with version history, and an external drive.

cards.d: Hauwa keeps working files, a cloud copy with version history, and an external drive.
Cloud storage plus a 1 TB external hard drive. She sized the cloud plan for 12 months of growth.
Monthly she copies to the drive, unplugs it and keeps it off-site. Each quarter she tests a restore.

say: On 2 types of storage. The folder is 40 gigabytes and grows about 2 a month, so in 12 months it will be 64. She chooses a cloud plan of at least 100.

say: With 1 copy off-site. Ransomware can encrypt any drive left plugged in, so once a month she copies the folder, unplugs the drive and takes it away.
Every quarter she restores a few files and opens them, and records the date and result. Many teams find out too late that their backup stopped months ago.

say: Email takeover is the most common incident, so write this playbook first. Step one. From a clean device, change the password to a new unique one.

panel.heading: When an email account is hacked
items: From a clean device, change the password
Turn on app or passkey MFA
Warn contacts and log every action

say: Step two. Sign out every other session.

say: Step three. Check for forwarding addresses, filters and auto-replies the attacker added. Screenshot them first, with date and time, because banks, police and regulators may need them. Then remove them.

say: For example, Ifeoma is volunteer IT lead for a parents' association in Lagos, with a spreadsheet of 420 families. At 14:00 on Tuesday, a committee member says she signed in on a strange page. Ifeoma logs it. That is the moment of awareness.
By 14:20 she has changed the password, signed out all sessions, and found and removed a forwarding rule, after a screenshot.
The attacker had opened the family spreadsheet. Phone numbers and children's details could enable targeted scams, so this is a reportable breach.
72 hours from Tuesday 14:00 is Friday 14:00. She notifies the NDPC on Thursday, and warns parents to ignore calls asking for money or codes.
To remember. One long passphrase, and unique generated passwords for everything else. App codes and passkeys beat SMS. Keep 3-2-1 backups and test restores.
In an incident, screenshot the evidence, then contain. And the NDPC's 72-hour clock starts when you become aware.

panel.heading: Remember
items: One long passphrase, unique passwords elsewhere
App codes and passkeys beat SMS
